column1: # ZAP alert-rule dispositions for the nightly deep API scan
# (.github/workflows/dast-deep.yml), passed to the action as rules_file_name.
# Tab-separated, because that is what ZAP parses: <rule id><TAB><IGNORE |
# WARN | FAIL><TAB>(reason). A line separated by spaces is read as one field
# and silently does nothing, so tests/test_dast_workflows.py parses this file
# the way ZAP does and fails on a malformed line.
# EVERY LINE IS A NAMED RULE WITH A WRITTEN REASON, and the suite caps how many
# there may be. ZAP's `-I`, which passes every warning at once, is forbidden: it
# is every suppression here, un-reviewed and unwritten, and it would silently
# absorb the next rule that starts firing.
# NOTHING MAY BE SUPPRESSED HERE FOR BEING INCONVENIENT. The passive header
# rules in particular stay armed: they are the attacker's-eye view of what the
# /v1 surface actually sends. The suite names them and fails if any appears

column3: (Strict-Transport-Security Header Not Set - the scan target is a plain-http loopback instance started by the workflow; a deployed vault terminates TLS (creek_mcp/transport_posture.py refuses a routable bind without it), so over loopback http this rule can only report the CI harness back to itself)

(Absence of Anti-CSRF Tokens - an HTML-form control; /v1 serves no HTML and authenticates every route from an Authorization header that a cross-site form cannot set, and no route accepts a cookie credential)
(Modern Web Application - informational; it reports that a response looks like a JavaScript-driven page, and /v1 serves only JSON)
(Information Disclosure - Suspicious Comments - reads HTML and JavaScript comments for developer notes; /v1 serves neither, so its matches are ordinary English words inside JSON error strings)
